a 49-year-old woman presented with an 8-month history of progressively worsening neck stiffness, bilateral elbow posturing, and daily whole-body shaking events, triggered by fear and sensory stimuli and lasting for a few minutes. Upon hospitalization, she developed polyuria (more than 200 mL of urine per hour) and polydipsia.

daily whole-body shaking events, triggered by fear and sensory stimuli and lasting for a few minutes. In the emergency department, she experienced one of her habitual events triggered by lowering the rail of the bed, characterized by whole-body rhythmic shaking and severe autonomic dysfunction (desaturation, hypertension, and tachycardia) with preserved level of consciousness, lasting for 10 min and spontaneously abating. Treatment with diazepam, baclofen and intravenous pulse steroids minimally helped in decreasing the rigidity.

extractions.quote: SPS is a rare disorder characterized by rigidity, painful spasms and psychiatric manifestations. Autoantibodies inhibit inhibitory neurons [1 ]. Amphiphysin is a synaptic protein responsible for endocytosis of the vesicle membrane after release of GABA (Gamma-Aminobutyric Acid) from the axonal ends, against which antibodies cause the paraneoplastic variant of SPS, mainly associated with breast cancer.

Electromyography showed continuous muscle firing at rest and concomitant agonist and antagonist contraction in the examined muscles.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) of the brain showed a faint hyperintensity over the hypothalamus consistent with hyperemia (Fig. 1, 1), and a cervical spine MRI revealed a T2 signal abnormality extending from C1 to C6 consistent with transverse myelitis (TM) (Fig. 1, 2).
Inflammatory and infectious etiologies of myelopathy were ruled out.
